content.text: When you see a rainbow arching across the sky after a rain shower, you are witnessing one of nature's most beautiful demonstrations of a physics phenomenon called dispersion. Dispersion is the separation of white light into its component colours as it passes through a medium such as glass or water. This seemingly simple phenomenon reveals a profound truth: what we perceive as white light is actually a mixture of many different colours, each with its own wavelength, and these different wavelengths interact with matter in slightly different ways.

Isaac Newton was the first to systematically study dispersion in the 1660s. He showed that a glass prism could split white light into a band of colours and, crucially, that these colours could be recombined to form white light again. This proved that the prism was not adding colour to the light but was revealing the colours already present within it.

In this lesson, we will explore the composition of white light, understand why different colours refract by different amounts, learn about the visible spectrum, and investigate colour addition and subtraction. These concepts are fundamental to understanding how we perceive colour and how colour is used in technology.

White light, such as sunlight or the light from an ordinary incandescent bulb, is not a single colour. It is a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum. When all these colours enter our eyes together, our brain perceives the combination as white. The individual colours that make up white light range from red (with the longest wavelength) to violet (with the shortest wavelength).

When a beam of white light enters a glass prism, it is refracted at the first surface. Because the refractive index of glass is slightly different for each colour (wavelength) of light, each colour is refracted by a slightly different amount. Violet light, which has the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum, is slowed down the most in glass and therefore has the highest refractive index. As a result, violet light is bent the most. Red light, with the longest wavelength, has the lowest refractive index in glass and is bent the least.

At the first surface of the prism, the colours begin to separate slightly. At the second surface, which is angled relative to the first, each colour is refracted again, and the separation increases. The result is a band of colours spread out in order of wavelength, known as a spectrum.
The key points about prism dispersion are:
Violet light is deviated the most (it has the highest refractive index in glass).
Red light is deviated the least (it has the lowest refractive index in glass).
The spectrum produced is: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (from least deviated to most deviated).
Dispersion occurs because the refractive index of the medium depends on the wavelength of light.

Although the difference seems small, the cumulative effect of refraction at both surfaces of a prism is enough to produce a clearly visible separation of colours.

This dependence of refractive index on wavelength is called chromatic dispersion and is a fundamental property of all transparent media (except a vacuum, where all wavelengths travel at exactly the same speed).

Newton demonstrated that the spectrum produced by one prism could be recombined into white light by using a second prism oriented in the opposite direction. When the dispersed colours pass through the second prism, the different amounts of refraction are reversed, bringing all the colours back together to form white light.
Another way to recombine colours is to use a converging lens to focus the dispersed spectrum to a point. At the focal point, all the colours overlap, and white light is observed.

This recombination experiment was crucial historically because it proved that white light is a genuine mixture of colours, and the prism does not create or change the colours but merely separates them.

Colour addition is the process of combining coloured lights. When lights of different colours are projected onto the same spot on a white screen, the overlapping region appears as a new colour. This is how television screens, computer monitors, and phone displays produce a full range of colours using only three primary colours of light.
These are called additive primary colours because they add together to produce other colours.

This is why colour screens use tiny red, green, and blue sub-pixels. By varying the brightness of each sub-pixel, any colour visible to the human eye can be produced.

Colour subtraction is the process of removing colours from white light. This occurs when light passes through colour filters or when light is reflected from coloured surfaces. The filter or pigment absorbs certain wavelengths and transmits or reflects the remaining wavelengths.
This is the basis of colour printing, which uses cyan, magenta, yellow, and black (CMYK) inks.
A colour filter is a piece of transparent material that transmits light of certain wavelengths while absorbing others. For example:
A red filter transmits red light and absorbs all other colours.
A blue filter transmits blue light and absorbs all other colours.
A green filter transmits green light and absorbs all other colours.

When white light passes through a red filter, only the red component is transmitted. Everything else is absorbed by the filter. If you then place a blue filter after the red filter, the red light that passed through the first filter is absorbed by the blue filter (which only transmits blue), and no light gets through. The combination appears black.
The colour of a transparent object (like a filter or stained glass) depends on which wavelengths it transmits. The colour of an opaque object depends on which wavelengths it reflects.
The colour of an object depends on the wavelengths of light it reflects (or transmits) into your eyes:
A red object reflects red light and absorbs most other colours.
A white object reflects all colours equally.
A black object absorbs all colours and reflects very little light.
This explains why objects can appear to change colour under different lighting:
A red object illuminated by red light appears red (because it reflects the red light).
A red object illuminated by blue light appears black (because there is no red light to reflect, and the blue light is absorbed).
A blue object under green light appears black (the blue object absorbs green light and there is no blue light to reflect).
A rainbow is a natural display of dispersion caused by sunlight interacting with water droplets in the atmosphere. The process involves three steps:
Sunlight enters a spherical raindrop and is refracted at the front surface. This refraction begins to separate the colours because different wavelengths are bent by different amounts.
The light hits the back surface of the raindrop and is reflected internally (total internal reflection or partial reflection).
The reflected light exits the raindrop through the front surface, being refracted again. This second refraction further separates the colours.

The combined effect of the two refractions and one internal reflection causes the light to emerge from the raindrop spread into a spectrum of colours. Because each colour emerges at a slightly different angle, an observer on the ground sees different colours coming from raindrops at different positions in the sky. Red light comes from drops higher in the sky (at an angle of about 42 degrees from the anti-solar point), and violet light comes from drops lower in the sky (at about 40 degrees). This is why the outer edge of a rainbow is red and the inner edge is violet.

Sometimes, a secondary rainbow is visible outside the primary one. This is caused by light undergoing two internal reflections inside the raindrops. The secondary rainbow is fainter and has the colour order reversed (red on the inside, violet on the outside).

Example 1: Identifying the Most Deviated Colour
White light passes through a glass prism. Which colour is deviated the most and which the least? Explain why.

Violet light is deviated the most because it has the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum and therefore the highest refractive index in glass. A higher refractive index means the light is bent more upon refraction.
Red light is deviated the least because it has the longest wavelength and therefore the lowest refractive index in glass.
The order from most deviated to least deviated is: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red.
White light passes through a cyan filter and then through a yellow filter. What colour emerges?
White light contains all colours: red, green, and blue (thinking in terms of the three primary colours).
A cyan filter absorbs red and transmits green and blue. After the cyan filter, the light contains green and blue.
A yellow filter absorbs blue and transmits red and green. The light entering the yellow filter contains green and blue. The blue is absorbed, and the green is transmitted.
The colour that emerges is green.
A yellow object is illuminated by (a) white light, (b) yellow light, (c) blue light. What colour does it appear in each case?
A yellow object reflects yellow light (which consists of red and green wavelengths) and absorbs blue light.
(a) Under white light (which contains all colours), the yellow object reflects the red and green components and absorbs the blue component. It appears yellow.
(b) Under yellow light, the object reflects the yellow light. It appears yellow.
(c) Under blue light, there is no red or green light to reflect. The object absorbs the blue light. Since no light is reflected, the object appears black.

A stage has three spotlights: one red, one green, and one blue. (a) What colour is produced where the red and green beams overlap? (b) What colour is produced where all three beams overlap? (c) What colour is produced where the blue and green beams overlap?
(a) Red + Green = Yellow (b) Red + Green + Blue = White (c) Blue + Green = Cyan

Misconception 1: A prism adds colour to white light

The prism does not create colours. The colours are already present in white light. The prism merely separates them because each colour (wavelength) has a slightly different refractive index in the glass material.
Misconception 2: The primary colours of light are red, yellow, and blue

The primary colours of light (additive primaries) are red, green, and blue, not red, yellow, and blue. Red, yellow, and blue are sometimes taught as primary colours for paint mixing (subtractive mixing), but even in that context, the true subtractive primaries are cyan, magenta, and yellow.
Misconception 3: Mixing all colours of paint produces white

Mixing all colours of paint (pigment) does not produce white; it produces a dark muddy colour close to black. This is because paint mixing is subtractive: each pigment absorbs more wavelengths, and when many pigments are mixed, almost all wavelengths are absorbed. Mixing all colours of light (additive mixing) produces white.
Misconception 4: Red objects contain red light

A red object does not contain red light or emit red light (unless it is a light source). Rather, it reflects red wavelengths and absorbs other wavelengths from whatever light illuminates it. Under blue illumination, a red object appears black because there are no red wavelengths available to reflect.
Misconception 5: The rainbow has exactly seven distinct colours

The spectrum is continuous, with one colour blending smoothly into the next. Newton chose to name seven colours to draw an analogy with the seven notes of a musical scale, but in reality, there are infinitely many shades in the spectrum. The boundary between, say, yellow and green is not sharp.

White light is a mixture of all colours (wavelengths) of the visible spectrum.
Dispersion is the separation of white light into its component colours due to the wavelength dependence of the refractive index.

A prism disperses white light because violet light (shortest wavelength) has the highest refractive index and is deviated the most, while red light (longest wavelength) has the lowest refractive index and is deviated the least.
The visible spectrum, in order of decreasing wavelength, is: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (ROYGBIV).
The primary colours of light (additive) are red, green, and blue. Combining all three in equal amounts produces white light.
The secondary colours of light are cyan (green + blue), magenta (red + blue), and yellow (red + green).
The primary colours of pigments (subtractive) are cyan, magenta, and yellow. Combining all three produces black.
Colour filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and transmitting others.
The colour of an object depends on which wavelengths it reflects; this can change under different illumination.
Rainbows are caused by dispersion, internal reflection, and refraction of sunlight in water droplets.
Violet light has a shorter wavelength than red light. In glass, shorter wavelengths travel more slowly, giving violet light a higher refractive index than red light. According to Snell's law (

), a higher refractive index in the glass means a smaller angle of refraction, which corresponds to greater bending towards the normal. Therefore, violet light is deviated more than red light when passing through the prism.

No light is observed (black). The red filter transmits only red light, absorbing all other wavelengths. The green filter transmits only green light and absorbs red. Since only red light reaches the green filter, and the green filter absorbs red, no light passes through.
A white object reflects all wavelengths:
(a) Under white light: appears white (reflects all colours).
(b) Under red light: appears red (reflects the red light).
(c) Under green light: appears green (reflects the green light).
A green object reflects only green light and absorbs others:
(a) Under white light: appears green (reflects only green).
(b) Under red light: appears black (absorbs red, no green to reflect).
(c) Under green light: appears green (reflects green).

Sunlight (white light) enters a spherical raindrop and is refracted at the front surface. Because the refractive index of water depends on wavelength, different colours refract by slightly different amounts, beginning the separation. The light then reflects off the back surface of the raindrop by internal reflection. On exiting through the front surface, the light is refracted a second time, further separating the colours. Red light emerges at a slightly larger angle (about 42°) from the anti-solar point than violet light (about 40°), so an observer sees red from higher drops and violet from lower drops, producing the characteristic order: red on the outside, violet on the inside.

Magenta light consists of red and blue (no green). A cyan object reflects blue and green, and absorbs red. Of the incident magenta light (red + blue), the red is absorbed and the blue is reflected. The object appears blue.
